children.text: Vigan Cathedral is the leading church of Ilocos Sur, built by the Augustinians around 1790–1800 and known for its thick earthquake-resisting buttresses and a separate octagonal bell tower. It is within walking distance of Plaza Salcedo and Calle Crisologo, which makes it a natural starting point for exploring Vigan.

The cathedral's formal name is the Metropolitan Cathedral of the Conversion of Saint Paul the Apostle. Locally it is also called Simbaan a Dakkel, Ilocano for "the big church." It is the seat of the Archdiocese of Nueva Segovia and the central landmark of the Historic City of Vigan, which became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999. It stands directly across from Plaza Salcedo, so it is usually the first building visitors notice in town.

The church traces back to 1574, when the Spanish conquistador Juan de Salcedo named the area Villa Fernandina and ordered a temporary church of wood and thatch. On April 30, 1575, the Augustinian chapter decided to build a permanent church and convent, and Vigan became the first parish in Northern Luzon. A church built in 1641 was repeatedly damaged by earthquakes and fire. On September 7, 1758, the seat of the Diocese of Nueva Segovia moved from present-day Lal-lo, Cagayan, to Vigan, and the church became a cathedral. The present building is the fourth church on the site: it was planned in 1786 on the order of Governor-General José Basco and built over roughly ten years starting in 1790.

The style is so-called Earthquake Baroque, designed for a country with frequent quakes. Unlike other Ilocos churches built of coral stone, it is made of adobe brick, with huge buttresses lined along its sides. The façade is Baroque with touches of Romanesque, Neo-Gothic and Chinese-inspired ornament, and a statue of Saint Paul in the central niche, shown with a horse, tells the story of his conversion. Like many old churches, its sheer thickness is far more impressive up close than in photos.

The cathedral was badly damaged by the magnitude 7.0 earthquake that struck northern Luzon on July 27, 2022. News reports described a displaced entrance, large cracks inside, broken roof beams and fallen statues. Repairs have continued since, so some areas may still have scaffolding or restricted access. Before you go, check the cathedral's official Facebook page or call to confirm what is open.

The thick buttresses supporting the sides are the cathedral's defining feature. The Baroque façade mixes Romanesque, Neo-Gothic and Chinese-style patterns, so it rewards a close look at the details. At dusk the walls glow golden, which makes for good photos.

blocks.title: A bell tower standing apart from the church

children.text: The bell tower stands separately, about
from the main church on the Plaza Burgos side. It is a three-storey octagonal tower roughly
high, topped by a rooster weather vane said to symbolize Saint Peter. It is explained as deliberately detached so it would not fall onto the church in an earthquake.

blocks.title: A silver-paneled altar and three retablos

children.text: The sanctuary has three Neo-Baroque retablos decorated with silver panels. The left one is dedicated to Apo Nazareno (the Black Nazarene), the right to Apo Birhen del Rosario (Our Lady of the Rosary), and the central main altar is said to date from the 19th century. Each column in the aisles carries a painting of one of the Twelve Apostles.

Two intricate wrought-iron pulpits face each other and are well preserved. Some of the stained glass comes from the old church and is mixed with plain panes that replaced broken ones. The floor is laid with baldosa tiles made in San Nicolas, Ilocos Norte.

The mortar holding the adobe bricks is said to be mixed with egg whites and molasses. The roof uses tegula tiles, reportedly the first of their kind in the Ilocos region, and the ceiling has a ribbed structure. A guide, if available, can explain these details at length.

blocks.title: The archbishop's palace and diocesan museum

children.text: To the left of the cathedral stands the Spanish colonial Archbishop's Palace of Nueva Segovia. It is described as the only surviving colonial-era archbishop's palace in the Philippines and houses a chapel, the archdiocesan archives and an ecclesiastical museum of artifacts from churches across Ilocos Sur. The chapel is usually open to the public.

The grave marker of the Ilocano poet Leona Florentino (1849–1884) is on a column near the side door facing Plaza Burgos. Bishop Juan de la Fuente Yepes, who asked for the see to be moved to Vigan, was reburied in a room beside the main altar in 1995, and several other bishops are also buried in the cathedral.
On the feast of Saint Paul,
January 25

, all the bells of the tower ring. After falling silent for a while following the 2022 earthquake, the bells rang again on January 25, 2025, and on weekends they were reported to ring at Angelus time. Check local announcements for exact ringing times.

items.title: 1–2 hour route
items.subtitle: From the plaza to the cathedral

children.text: Arrive for the early morning Mass or soon after. There are fewer people and the soft light is good for photographing the façade.
First look at the façade from Plaza Salcedo, then walk around the buttressed sides and the bell tower. The plaza holds the Juan de Salcedo monument and the Vigan Dancing Fountain.
If no Mass is in progress, step inside and take your time with the silver retablos, the paintings of the Twelve Apostles and the wrought-iron pulpits. Do not enter areas under repair.
If the archbishop's palace chapel and diocesan museum are open, take a look. Opening hours are not fixed, so check on the spot.
Walk to Calle Crisologo for breakfast or an empanada.
The cathedral is a place of worship, so during Mass avoid photography and loud conversation, and move quietly.

items.title: Half-day Vigan route
items.subtitle: From the cathedral to the historic district

children.text: Look around the cathedral and the bell tower. Many visitors say the façade looks golden in late-afternoon light.
Visit nearby museums such as Padre Burgos House. Many are free to enter but accept donations.
Walk along Calle Crisologo and try a horse-drawn calesa ride.
Watch the fountain at Plaza Salcedo and have dinner.
The overland trip from Manila or Quezon City to Vigan takes about
7–10 hours
, via MacArthur Highway or the Manila North Road.
Dominion, Partas, Viron and St. Joseph run buses to Vigan. Wikivoyage lists the Dominion fare as
, but that is 2017 information and fares are likely higher now. Check the current fare at the terminal.
As of September 2023, Vigan's airport had no scheduled flights. The nearest airport is Laoag International Airport, served from Manila by Philippine Airlines and others, and Laoag is about
1 hour 30 minutes
from Vigan by car.
A rental car or a car with driver makes it easy to combine Vigan with northern Ilocos.
The cathedral sits beside Plaza Salcedo in the historic district, so you can get around on foot.
Tricycles in town cost about
according to Wikivoyage, a calesa (horse-drawn carriage) about
per hour, and a full day of 6–7 hours about
. Negotiate or confirm the fare before you ride.
The cathedral can be visited all year, but the dry season is better for staying out of the rain and walking comfortably. In Ilocos, November to April is relatively dry and sunny.

Around the January 25 feast of Saint Paul, the Longganisa Festival (January 22), the Binatbatan Festival in the first week of May and Holy Week, events draw crowds and rooms fill up early. For a quiet visit, pick a weekday morning.

Staying inside the historic district, within walking distance of the cathedral, makes an early-morning visit easy. Wikivoyage lists budget places such as Vigan Hotel at
, Casa Teofila at
and Villa Angela Heritage House at
. Prices vary widely by season.

Typical foods are Vigan longganisa, Vigan empanada, miki noodles, okoy (shrimp fritters) and sinanglao (beef innards soup). On the street you can try tinubong (sticky rice cake in bamboo tubes) and cornick, and the sugarcane wine basi is famous. Wikivoyage names shops such as Insiang's Empanada, First Sinanglaoan, Tongson's Royal Bibingka and Calle Brewery.

Entry is free, but opening hours differ between sources. Some say the doors open around 7 AM, so go in the morning and confirm by phone at (077) 722-2644 or (077) 674-2392, or on the official Facebook page.
Mass schedules change often. One review lists weekday Masses at 6–7 AM and 5:15–6:15 PM and several on Sundays, so rely on the official announcement first.
Visiting during Mass shows the church as it really is, but be careful with photography. Dress modestly, covering shoulders and knees.
Many reviews say the façade is best in late-afternoon light, and the fire trees around the bell tower are loveliest when in bloom.
You can hire a calesa from the carriage stand in front of the church to link Calle Crisologo and other sights. Agree on time and fare before boarding.
If a guide is on hand, ask about the building materials and history for a much deeper understanding. Tips or donations are optional.
Repair work may mean scaffolding or cordons. Do not enter restricted areas and follow the signs.
The fountain show is better seen in the evening. According to Wikivoyage, Plaza Salcedo is open from 7 AM to 7:30 PM.

The magnitude 7.0 earthquake of July 2022 severely damaged the cathedral and bell tower, and they were once closed under the highest level, Code Red. Some areas may still be under repair, so be sure to check whether it is open before your visit.
Access inside the bell tower may be restricted for structural safety. Do not rely on older reviews saying you can climb it.
Parts of the church close during services, weddings and funerals.
Fees, opening hours and Mass times differ between sources, so confirm them locally.
It is very hot and the sun is strong at midday, so bring a hat and water.
On crowded feast days and during Holy Week, watch for pickpockets and inflated prices.
Right in front of the cathedral, with the Juan de Salcedo monument and the Vigan Dancing Fountain. It is a

walk.
Vigan's signature street, lined with Spanish-style stone houses, is about
5–10 minutes
on foot from the cathedral. The cobblestones make for pleasant walking.
A history museum in Vigan close to the cathedral; according to Wikivoyage it is free, with donations accepted.
Another Baroque church in Ilocos, regarded as similar to Vigan Cathedral. Reach it from Vigan by road.
A Spanish-era church and watchtower near Vigan. Access was reported to be restricted after the 2022 earthquake, so check before you go.
